content.title: Joining Independent Clauses with Coordinating Conjunctions
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the specific punctuation rule for joining two independent clauses using a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS). Mastering this rule prevents run-on sentences and comma splices, which are frequently tested on the ACT English section.
learning_objectives: Identify independent clauses within a compound sentence.
Apply the rule for placing a comma before a coordinating conjunction when it joins two independent clauses.
Distinguish between compound sentences and sentences with compound predicates that do not require a comma.

sections.title: The FANBOYS Conjunctions
sections.content: Coordinating conjunctions are words used to connect grammatically equal elements. There are exactly seven: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, and So. An easy way to remember them is the acronym FANBOYS. In the context of this lesson, we use these words to link two complete thoughts together into one sentence.

sections.title: The Independent Clause Test
sections.content: An independent clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought; it can stand alone as a sentence. Before placing a comma before a FANBOYS word, you must verify that both the preceding group of words and the following group of words are independent clauses. If either side cannot stand alone as a complete sentence, the comma is usually unnecessary.

sections.title: The Comma-Before-FANBOYS Rule
sections.content: When a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS) joins two independent clauses, you must place a comma immediately before the conjunction. The formula is: [Independent Clause] + [,] + [FANBOYS] + [Independent Clause]. Failure to include the comma results in a run-on sentence.

worked_examples.question: Identify the correct punctuation for the following sentence: 'The marathon was exhausting yet every runner managed to cross the finish line.'
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the first clause: 'The marathon was exhausting.' This has a subject (marathon) and a verb (was) and is a complete thought. Step 2: Identify the second clause: 'every runner managed to cross the finish line.' This has a subject (runner) and a verb (managed) and is a complete thought. Step 3: Identify the conjunction: 'yet'. Step 4: Apply the rule. Since both sides are independent clauses, a comma must be placed before 'yet'. Corrected: 'The marathon was exhausting, yet every runner managed to cross the finish line.'

worked_examples.question: Determine if a comma is needed: 'The chef prepared a five-course meal and served it to the guests.'
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the first part: 'The chef prepared a five-course meal.' This is an independent clause. Step 2: Identify the second part: 'served it to the guests.' This lacks a subject (who served it?). It is a predicate, not an independent clause. Step 3: Apply the rule. Since the second part is not an independent clause, no comma is needed before 'and'. Corrected: 'The chef prepared a five-course meal and served it to the guests.'

common_mistakes: Placing a comma before every 'and' or 'but' regardless of what follows it.
Forgetting the comma when the two independent clauses are very short (e.g., 'I ran and he walked' still requires a comma: 'I ran, and he walked').
Using a semicolon instead of a comma before a FANBOYS word (e.g., 'Clause; but Clause' is incorrect).
exam_tips: Always check the words after the FANBOYS. If there is no new subject, you likely don't need a comma.
If you see a comma and a FANBOYS word underlined, check if the sentence can be split into two logical sentences at that point.
The ACT often uses 'so' and 'but' to test this rule because they frequently start new independent clauses.
content.recap: To join two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS), you must place a comma before the conjunction. If the conjunction is not joining two independent clauses, do not use a comma.

knowledge_claims.content: An independent clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb that can stand alone as a complete sentence.
The seven coordinating conjunctions are For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, and So (FANBOYS).
A comma must be placed immediately before a coordinating conjunction when it connects two independent clauses.
To determine if a comma is needed before a FANBOYS word, test if the words on both sides of the conjunction can stand alone as separate sentences.
It is a mistake to omit the comma when a coordinating conjunction joins two independent clauses, as this creates a run-on sentence.
It is a mistake to place a comma before a coordinating conjunction if the following phrase lacks a subject and cannot stand alone.
Unlike a semicolon, which can join two independent clauses alone, a coordinating conjunction requires a preceding comma to join two independent clauses.
In the sentence 'He liked the movie, but he hated the book,' the comma is required because 'he hated the book' is an independent clause.
In the sentence 'He liked the movie but hated the book,' no comma is used because 'hated the book' is not an independent clause.
A valid check for this rule is to replace the comma and FANBOYS with a period; if two complete sentences remain, the comma was necessary.
The comma-before-FANBOYS rule applies even if the independent clauses are short, such as 'It rained, so we stayed.'
The word 'so' functions as a coordinating conjunction when it means 'therefore' and joins two independent clauses.

ENGLISH PASSAGE 1: The Clock Above Alder Street
[1] After three months of fundraising [[a neighborhood restoration crew began]] to repair the brass clock above Alder Street Market. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a market hall built in 1911, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using a laser scan and a box of hand-labeled gears, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] wear marks showed that an earlier repairer had reversed two nearly identical wheels. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because replacement parts would have erased those clues. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the crew cleaned and reused the original wheels. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the clock kept accurate time through a week of rain. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the repair preserved evidence of how local mechanics once solved problems.]]

Which choice correctly punctuates the wording marked [6]?
F) , it instead treated the problem as useful evidence
G) ; it instead treated the problem as useful evidence
H) : and it instead treated the problem as useful evidence
J)  it instead, treated the problem as useful evidence

options.A: , it instead treated the problem as useful evidence
options.B: ; it instead treated the problem as useful evidence
options.C: : and it instead treated the problem as useful evidence
options.D: it instead, treated the problem as useful evidence

items.explanation: A semicolon correctly joins the two closely related independent clauses.

ENGLISH PASSAGE 2: Counting After Dark
[1] After several cloudy evenings [[a coastal ecology class began]] to count juvenile crabs in tide pools after sunset. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a protected inlet beside the school, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using red lamps, quadrats, and waterproof tally sheets, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] the smallest crabs appeared most often under flat stones near eelgrass. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because bright white light changed the animals’ movement. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the class switched to dim red lamps and repeated the first survey. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the second set of counts was more consistent. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the revised method gave park staff a dependable baseline for future surveys.]]

Which choice correctly punctuates the wording marked [6]?
F) , it instead treated the problem as useful evidence
G) : and it instead treated the problem as useful evidence
H)  it instead, treated the problem as useful evidence
J) ; it instead treated the problem as useful evidence

options.A: , it instead treated the problem as useful evidence
options.B: : and it instead treated the problem as useful evidence
options.C: it instead, treated the problem as useful evidence
options.D: ; it instead treated the problem as useful evidence

videoLesson.title: Revise With Comma Before FANBOYS
videoLesson.description: Recognize when both sides of a conjunction contain complete clauses with subjects and verbs. If both are independent clauses, place a comma immediately before the coordinating conjunction; otherwise omit it.
